title: the ocean the wave forgets it is
hookLine: a proud son, a lump of salt in water, and the whole that's in every sip
tomorrow: anyone who turns a light on

lines: HOME AFTER TWELVE YEARS, SURE OF HIMSELF.
A LUMP OF SALT. A CUP OF WATER.
cards: A young man comes home after twelve years of study, very sure of himself. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question he can't answer, and starts teaching him again.
One day he hands him a lump of salt: put this in a cup of water, and come back in the morning. The son, Shvetaketu, does. Next morning the father says: bring me the salt.
The boy looks. It's gone. Sip from the top, says the father.

teach.b: Brahman. Not Brahma, the creator god in the stories, and not Brahmin, the priestly class. Different words.
Brahman is the name the Upanishads give to the whole: the reality underneath everything, what everything comes from and returns to.

teach.h: SALT IN WATER, RIVERS IN THE SEA
teach.b: Like the salt, it isn't one more thing you can pick out. It's in every taste. The same chapter of the Chandogya has another picture.
Rivers flow, some east, some west, and in the end they reach the sea and become the sea. And once there, the Upanishad says, they don't know: I am this river, I am that one.
Now the line the father keeps saying to his son, again and again in that chapter: tat tvam asi.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI — THAT'S WHAT YOU ARE
teach.b: That's what you are. Yesterday's word, atman, the self, and today's word, Brahman, the whole: the Upanishad brings them face to face.
Hindu thinkers read the line in more than one way. Advaita Vedanta, taught by Shankara, reads it as identity: the self and the whole are not two.

Ramanuja's school reads it as one whole with real differences inside it, the self living in God and God as the self's inner ruler. Madhva's school keeps the self and God distinct, the self always dependent on God.
These readings sit side by side in the tradition, and nobody here has to choose. Just notice what the picture does.

In the Upanishad, the rivers don't dry up somewhere along the way. They become the sea. And today's title borrows the picture for one way of hearing it: a wave that is ocean the whole time, even while it forgets.
And it's one root of things you'll see in Hindu life: bowing to a river, honoring a guest, greeting someone with folded hands. For many Hindus, the same reality is in all of it.

how: Hindus study the Upanishads' teaching on Brahman with teachers and commentaries, and the schools of Vedanta (Shankara's Advaita, Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, Madhva's Dvaita) each read 'tat tvam asi' in their own way.

games.q: Sam asked Nani: if god is in everything, is my DOG god?? 😂 Nani laughed so hard she couldn't answer. what's the real answer
o: the Upanishads say the whole, Brahman, is in everything, like salt in every sip. so yes, in your dog too. schools explain it different ways.
no, god is only in temples and statues.
yes, your dog is Brahma the creator.
games.why: Uddalaka showed that the salt is in every sip though it can't be picked out. Brahman, the whole, is in everything; Hindu schools read 'that's what you are' in different ways.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a creator god in the stories

s: Brahman and Brahma are the same word
Brahma is a creator god in the stories; Brahman is the Upanishads' word for the whole.
Hindu schools read tat tvam asi in more than one way
Shankara reads it as not two; Ramanuja and Madhva read it differently.
in the story, the salt simply disappears
it can't be picked out, but every sip, top to bottom, tastes of it.

games.q: you're Shvetaketu. your father asks for the salt you dropped in the water last night. you look in the cup. what do you find?
o: the salt, sitting at the bottom.
nothing to pick up, but every sip is salty.
plain water; the salt is gone for good.
games.why: the salt can't be found anywhere and can be tasted everywhere. that's how Uddalaka points at the whole: tat tvam asi, that's what you are.

practice: Here's the practice: let the river reach the sea. Sit and breathe. Bring a river to mind, any one you've seen or can imagine.
Let it carry this life, this name, today's worries. Follow it as it moves. Then let it reach the sea, and let the edges go.
Not lost: arrived. Rest there, in the big water. Some rest there with one name of God in mind.

wordCard.voice: Brahman. The whole, the reality under everything. Not Brahma, not Brahmin. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the whole, the reality underneath everything; not Brahma, the god.

carryVoice: Your line: not two. The salt is in every sip. When someone feels far from you today, remember what the Upanishad says is in them too. Day eleven.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–6.1.3 (Shvetaketu returns after twelve years, proud; his father questions him)
